questions.q: State the partial pressures of O₂ and CO₂ in atmospheric air, alveolar air, and deoxygenated blood arriving at the alveoli.
questions.a: Atmospheric air: pO₂ ≈ 159 mm Hg, pCO₂ ≈ 0.3 mm Hg. Alveolar air: pO₂ ≈ 104 mm Hg, pCO₂ ≈ 40 mm Hg. Deoxygenated (pulmonary arterial) blood: pO₂ ≈ 40 mm Hg, pCO₂ ≈ 45 mm Hg. A wrong answer (e.g., thinking alveolar pO₂ equals atmospheric 159 mm Hg) reveals the student hasn't grasped that alveolar air is a mixture of fresh inspired air and residual air, so its composition differs from atmospheric air.

questions.q: Why does CO₂ diffuse from blood to alveoli even though its partial pressure gradient (5 mm Hg) is much smaller than that of O₂ (64 mm Hg)?
questions.a: CO₂ is 20–25 times more soluble in the diffusion membrane than O₂. According to Fick’s Law, diffusion rate is proportional to (partial pressure gradient × solubility). The high solubility compensates for the smaller gradient, allowing CO₂ to diffuse at a similar rate as O₂. A student who says "CO₂ gradient is larger" or "CO₂ is lighter" confuses partial pressure values or molecular weight with solubility.

questions.q: A patient has pulmonary fibrosis thickening the alveolar-capillary membrane to 2 µm (normal ≈ 0.5 µm). Predict the effect on O₂ and CO₂ exchange and explain why CO₂ exchange might be less affected initially.
questions.a: O₂ exchange will decrease significantly because diffusion rate is inversely proportional to membrane thickness (Fick’s Law). CO₂ exchange is less affected because its much higher solubility (20–25×) partially offsets the increased diffusion distance. A wrong answer claiming both gases are equally affected ignores the solubility factor; a student saying CO₂ is more affected confuses the direction of the gradient.

questions.q: Compare the composition of alveolar air with atmospheric air and expired air. Explain why alveolar pO₂ is lower and pCO₂ higher than atmospheric air.
questions.a: Alveolar air: pO₂ 104 mm Hg, pCO₂ 40 mm Hg. Atmospheric air: pO₂ 159 mm Hg, pCO₂ 0.3 mm Hg. Expired air: pO₂ ~116 mm Hg, pCO₂ ~32 mm Hg. Alveolar pO₂ is lower because O₂ continuously diffuses into blood; alveolar pCO₂ is higher because CO₂ continuously diffuses from blood. The dead space air (no gas exchange) dilutes expired air toward atmospheric values. A student who thinks alveolar air equals expired air forgets the mixing with dead space air.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "In the alveoli, O₂ binds to haemoglobin because the pO₂ is high; in tissues, O₂ is released because pO₂ is low." Is this a complete explanation of the loading and unloading of O₂?
questions.a: The statement is incomplete. While partial pressure is the primary factor, the Bohr effect (pCO₂, H⁺ concentration, temperature) shifts the oxygen dissociation curve. In tissues, high pCO₂, high H⁺, and higher temperature further promote O₂ release beyond what pO₂ alone would cause. In alveoli, low pCO₂, low H⁺, and lower temperature enhance binding. A student who agrees fully misses the allosteric regulation of haemoglobin – a key Class 11 concept covered in node 004.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a spirometer and gas analysis to demonstrate that alveolar air composition remains relatively constant during normal breathing, while inspired and expired air differ.
questions.a: Collect inspired air (via a valve), expired air (mixed), and end-tidal air (last 100 mL of expiration, approximating alveolar air) during spirometry. Analyse O₂ and CO₂ percentages with a gas analyser. Expected: Inspired ≈ 21% O₂, 0.04% CO₂; End-tidal ≈ 14% O₂, 5.3% CO₂; Mixed expired ≈ 16% O₂, 4% CO₂. The end-tidal sample shows alveolar composition is stable and distinct. A poor design that only measures mixed expired air cannot isolate alveolar air, revealing confusion between dead space and respiratory zone.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Alveolar exchange is the process of passive diffusion of oxygen (O₂) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) across the ______ membrane (alveolar epithelium, capillary endothelium, and their fused basement membranes) driven by partial pressure gradients between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood.
Fill in the blank: Hold your breath for 30 seconds – the urge to breathe ______ from rising CO₂, not low O₂.
What is Alveolar exchange? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Alveolar exchange is the process of passive diffusion of oxygen (O₂) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) across the respiratory membrane (alveolar epithelium, capillary endothelium, and their fused basement membranes) driven by partial pressure gradients between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Hold your breath for ______ seconds – the urge to breathe comes from rising CO₂, not low O₂.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the direction of O₂ and CO₂ diffusion using partial pressure values from Table 14.1, describe the three-layered diffusion membrane, and justify why CO₂ diffuses faster than O₂ despite a smaller partial pressure gradient.
